page_contents_html:
Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is defined as any vaginal bleeding occurring 12 months or more after the last menstrual period. It requires investigation in all cases to exclude endometrial cancer.

Approximately 1 in 10 women with PMB will have endometrial cancer. The most common cause is urogenital atrophy (~60%), but the diagnosis of a benign cause cannot be assumed without investigation.

All women with PMB should be referred on a 2-week wait (suspected cancer) pathway regardless of age. Primary care investigation is limited to history, examination, and cervical screening if due — do not delay referral.

  • D&G WEST (Dumfries, Annandale, Nithsdale): One-stop PMB clinic — DGRI/Mountainhall Treatment Centre
  • D&G EAST (Galloway): GCH Gynaecology clinic — scan arranged separately

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Aim: Confirm PMB, identify relevant risk factors, and prepare information for the gynaecology referral. Do not delay referral to complete investigation in primary care.

History

  • Confirm timing: vaginal bleeding occurring ≥12 months after last menstrual period
  • Character of bleeding: onset, frequency, volume, associated pain or discharge
  • HRT use — type (sequential or continuous combined), duration, timing of last dose change
    • Sequential HRT: note whether bleeding occurs in the expected withdrawal window or is unscheduled
    • Continuous combined HRT: any bleeding is unscheduled and requires investigation
  • Anticoagulant medications: warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs — apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)
  • Other relevant medications: tamoxifen (increases endometrial cancer risk), corticosteroids
  • Cervical screening history — date and result of last smear
  • Personal or family history of HNPCC/Lynch syndrome, hereditary breast/ovarian cancer (BRCA)
  • Obesity (BMI >30): independent risk factor for endometrial cancer
  • Symptoms suggesting non-gynaecological source: haematuria (urological), rectal bleeding (bowel)

Examination

  • Abdominal palpation: assess for uterine or adnexal mass
  • Speculum examination:
    • Inspect vaginal walls — note atrophy, pallor, petechiae, friability
    • Inspect cervix — note polyps, contact bleeding, visible lesion, ulceration
    • Obtain cervical smear only if due — do not delay referral to perform smear
  • Bimanual pelvic examination if clinically appropriate — assess uterine size and mobility, adnexal tenderness or mass

Exclude non-gynaecological sources

  • Haematuria — check urinalysis; consider urology referral if confirmed
  • Rectal bleeding — confirm source on examination before attributing to bowel
  • Vulval pathology — inspect vulva; refer dermatology or gynaecology if suspicious lesion

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
The role of primary care management in PMB is very limited. Investigation and definitive management is led by gynaecology following referral. Do not initiate or trial treatments before referral.

Topical oestrogen for urogenital atrophy

  • May be offered if there is clear clinical evidence of urogenital atrophy on examination (pale, thin, friable vaginal walls)
  • Options: estriol vaginal cream or pessaries; oestradiol vaginal tablets or ring
  • Do not delay referral to trial topical oestrogen — prescribe alongside the 2WW referral, not instead of it
  • Topical oestrogen does not exclude endometrial pathology

HRT review

  • If on sequential HRT with unscheduled bleeding: review regimen (dose, duration of progestogen phase, compliance) — but still refer for investigation
  • Consider British Menopause Society guidance for managing HRT-related bleeding (NICE NG12 1.5.15)

Do not delay referral

Do not withhold 2WW referral to await a smear result, to trial topical oestrogen, or to adjust HRT. These can run in parallel with referral but must not substitute for it.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
2-Week Wait referral — ALL postmenopausal bleeding

  • Any unexplained vaginal bleeding ≥12 months after the last menstrual period — regardless of age, quantity, or apparent cause
  • HNPCC/Lynch syndrome carriers presenting with any PMB
  • PMB in women on tamoxifen
  • PMB where examination reveals a suspicious cervical lesion (consider urgent colposcopy in parallel)

Refer via 2WW (suspected cancer) pathway on SCI referrals. Do not await scan results before referring.

D&G referral destinations

  • WEST (Dumfries, Annandale, Nithsdale): One-stop PMB clinic — DGRI/Mountainhall Treatment Centre
    Transvaginal ultrasound scan + gynaecology review in same visit. Endometrial biopsy (Pipelle) as indicated.
  • EAST (Galloway): GCH Gynaecology clinic
    Urgent pelvic ultrasound scan arranged separately. Gynaecology review with scan result. Endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy as indicated.

Asymptomatic endometrial thickening (incidental finding)

  • Endometrial thickness >7mm found incidentally on pelvic ultrasound in a postmenopausal woman with no current PMB → refer to gynaecology (routine, not 2WW)
  • Can be referred to any gynaecology clinic (not necessarily one-stop PMB clinic)
  • Threshold may differ for women on HRT — seek gynaecology advice if uncertain

Evidence base

  • NICE NG12 (2015, updated 2023): Suspected cancer — recognition and referral
    • 1.5.12: Refer women ≥55 with unexplained PMB on 2WW pathway
    • 1.5.14: Refer women <55 with unexplained PMB not attributable to HRT on 2WW pathway
    • D&G practice: refer ALL PMB on 2WW regardless of age (consistent with NG12 as a whole)

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
There are very few situations in which referral can be safely withheld in PMB. The default position is to refer all PMB on a 2WW pathway.

Possible exception — sequential HRT withdrawal bleed

A single episode of light spotting occurring predictably in the expected withdrawal window on correctly-taken sequential HRT may not require 2WW referral if all of the following apply:

  • Bleeding is clearly in the progestogen-free phase (expected withdrawal window)
  • Pattern is unchanged from previous cycles on same HRT regimen
  • Recent pelvic ultrasound (within 12 months) showing normal endometrial thickness
  • No other concerning symptoms or risk factors (obesity, Lynch syndrome, tamoxifen)
  • GP and patient are both confident of the attribution

Even in this scenario, maintain a low threshold for referral if there is any doubt, the pattern changes, or bleeding recurs. Seek gynaecology telephone advice if uncertain.

NICE NG12 1.5.15 specifically notes limited evidence for HRT-related unscheduled bleeding and directs to British Menopause Society guidance.

Do not withhold referral because:

  • Bleeding was a single episode or small in volume
  • Atrophic vaginitis is clinically apparent — this does not exclude coexisting endometrial pathology
  • A cervical polyp has been identified
  • Patient is elderly or has significant comorbidity — discuss with gynaecology rather than withholding referral
  • Awaiting smear result or previous smear was normal
